usage: 돌다 is the natural verb; 모퉁이를 돌면 = once you round the corner
pointing it out when giving directions
narrow side-street corner, not a big intersection
examples: If you turn that corner, there's a convenience store.
돌면 = once you round it; classic direction sentence
Let's meet in front of the cafe on the corner.
using the corner shop as a meeting point
Go straight up to the corner from here.
까지 = up to; 쭉 = straight along
nuance: 모퉁이 is the corner where a road or building bends, the spot you round on foot. For a four-way intersection of cars you want 사거리 instead, and 모퉁이 feels smaller and more pedestrian. Koreans give directions by chaining 모퉁이를 돌면... (once you turn the corner), so it is one of the most useful walking-direction words.
mistakes: Using 모퉁이 for a big car intersection — that is 사거리 or 교차로
Saying 모서리 for a street corner; 모서리 is the sharp edge of an object like a table

english: the opposite side (right across, facing you)
usage: to be on the opposite side
바로 stresses it is straight across
examples: The bank is across from the convenience store.
Cross over to the opposite side over there.
The restaurant is right across from our office.
nuance: 맞은편 means the side directly facing you, as if the two spots stare at each other across a road or room. It is slightly more 'face-to-face' than 건너편, though in daily speech the two overlap heavily. Use it to pin a landmark: 약국 맞은편 (across from the pharmacy) tells someone exactly where to look.
mistakes: Confusing 맞은편 with 옆 (next to); 맞은편 is across, not beside
Forgetting the location particle — say 맞은편에 있어요, not just 맞은편 있어요

english: the other side (across the road or river)
usage: to go to the other side
to see from the other side
the far side of the river
across a river or wide road
examples: There's a big supermarket across the street.
To get to the other side, cross at the crosswalk.
으려면 = if you want to; pairs with crossing
My friend waved from across the way.
nuance: 건너편 is the side you reach by crossing something — a road, a river, the tracks — and it pairs naturally with 건너다 (to cross). It overlaps with 맞은편, but 건너편 emphasizes the act of crossing over to get there, while 맞은편 stresses simply facing you. For directions involving a crosswalk, 건너편 is the word locals reach for first.
mistakes: Using 건너편 when the place is on your own side; it must be across something you cross
Mixing it up with 다음 (next); 건너편 is across, not the next one along

usage: to cut through via the shortcut
examples: If you go this way, it's a shortcut.
If you know the shortcut, it's ten minutes faster.
There's a shortcut that cuts through the alley.
질러가다 + 지름길 are a natural pair
nuance: 지름길 is a shorter, faster route that skips the long way around, often through alleys or back streets a local would know. Figuratively it can also mean a 'fast track' to a goal (성공의 지름길 = the shortcut to success), so context decides. In navigation talk it pairs with 질러가다 (to cut across) and contrasts with 돌아가다 (to go the long way).
mistakes: Writing 지름낄 or 지름킬; the spelling is 지름길
Confusing it with 골목길 (alley) — an alley can be a shortcut, but 지름길 is specifically the shorter route

usage: at the fork in the road
examples: At the fork, go to the left.
If you go a bit, a fork comes up.
I'm standing at a crossroads in life right now.
figurative use; a big decision point
nuance: 갈림길 is the point where one road splits into two or more, the moment you must choose a direction. Literally it guides walking or driving (갈림길에서 오른쪽), but Koreans use it just as often for life's big decision points (인생의 갈림길). The verb 갈리다 (to be divided) is the root, so the image is a path branching apart.
mistakes: Confusing 갈림길 (a fork) with 사거리 (a four-way intersection); a fork splits, an intersection crosses
Spelling it 갈림낄 — the correct form is 갈림길

examples: Bicycles aren't allowed on the sidewalk.
The sidewalk was narrow, so we walked single file.
The sidewalk blocks are broken, so be careful.
nuance: 보도 is the formal word for the pedestrian walkway beside a road, the same thing as 인도. You will see 보도 on official signs and hear 인도 more in casual speech, but both are fine. The compound 보도블록 (sidewalk paving blocks) is everyday vocabulary because Korea's tiled sidewalks come up constantly in complaints and small talk.
mistakes: Confusing 보도 (sidewalk) with 차도 (the roadway for cars)
Reading 보도 as 'news report' — that is a different 보도 (報道); context makes the street meaning clear

usage: to go up onto the overpass
육교 usually means stairs to climb
examples: To cross the road, use the overpass.
The overpass has lots of stairs, so it's a bit tiring.
If there's no crosswalk, cross via the overpass.
으면 = if; 로 = by way of
nuance: 육교 is the raised footbridge that lets pedestrians cross over a busy road, the opposite of the underground 지하도. Older 육교 have lots of stairs and no elevator, so people with luggage or strollers often grumble about them. When there is no crosswalk nearby, taking the 육교 is the safe and legal way across.
mistakes: Confusing 육교 (overpass, you go up) with 지하도 (underpass, you go down)
Calling a big highway bridge 육교; a car bridge over a river is 다리, while 육교 is for pedestrians over a road

usage: to go down into the underpass
examples: Cross the road through the underpass over there.
If you go down into the underpass, it's cool.
I bought socks at the underground arcade.
nuance: 지하도 is the underground passage that takes pedestrians beneath a busy road or intersection, the counterpart to the elevated 육교. Many large 지하도 double as shopping arcades (지하도 상가), so locals duck into them to cross and to browse at the same time. Note it differs from 지하철 (subway), even though both start with 지하 (underground).
mistakes: Confusing 지하도 (pedestrian underpass) with 지하철 (subway train)
Mixing up 지하도 (you go down) with 육교 (you go up over the road)

usage: add 하다 to make the verb
examples: 우회전하다 = to make a right turn
It's a right turn at the next light.
Get into the right-turn lane in advance.
nuance: 우회전 is the driving and navigation term for a right turn (우 = right + 회전 = turning), the natural partner of 좌회전. You hear it constantly from GPS apps like 카카오내비 and Tmap, and as a passenger you can direct a taxi with 여기서 우회전해 주세요. On foot people more often just say 오른쪽으로 가세요, so 우회전 leans toward cars.
mistakes: Using 우회전 for walking directions; on foot say 오른쪽으로 (to the right)
Swapping 우회전 (right) and 좌회전 (left) — 우 is right, 좌 is left

usage: add 하다 to make the verb
the green arrow at a light
a sign term drivers must know
examples: Turn left at the next intersection.
좌회전하다 = to make a left turn
This is an unprotected left turn.
nuance: 좌회전 is the right turn's mirror image — a left turn (좌 = left + 회전 = turning) — and it is core driving and GPS vocabulary. The phrase 비보호 좌회전 (unprotected left turn, where you turn on green without a dedicated arrow) is worth knowing because it appears on real signs and trips up new drivers. As with 우회전, walkers usually just say 왼쪽으로 가세요.
mistakes: Confusing 좌회전 (left) with 우회전 (right); 좌 is left
Assuming every 좌회전 is on a green arrow — 비보호 좌회전 means you turn on a plain green light when clear

usage: add 하다 to make the verb
examples: This lane is for going straight only.
nuance: 직진 means proceeding straight ahead without turning, completing the trio with 우회전 and 좌회전 that you hear from every navigation app. Spoken commands chain them: 직진하다가 좌회전 (go straight, then turn left). On foot the casual equivalent is 쭉 가세요 or 똑바로 가세요, so 직진 itself sounds a touch more like driving or GPS speech.
mistakes: Pairing 직진 with the wrong verb — it takes 하다 (직진하다), not 가다 directly
Forgetting that lane signs limit movement; a 직진 차선 means you cannot turn from it

examples: It's one-way, so we have to go around.
I didn't see the one-way sign.
nuance: 일방통행 describes a road where traffic legally flows in only one direction, a constant feature of Korea's older, narrow neighborhood streets. Drivers and taxi passengers run into it often, and missing a 일방통행 표지판 (one-way sign) means an annoying detour (돌아가다). Knowing the word helps you understand why your GPS suddenly routes you the long way around.
mistakes: Confusing 일방통행 (one-way) with 양방향 통행 (two-way traffic) — 양방향 통행 is the standard term, not 양방통행
Thinking it only applies to cars; 일방통행 governs the road itself, so even cyclists must follow it
